The `Cerebro` data class formalizes the data structure to provide stability and improve backward compatibility across CerebroNexus releases.

While the data is organized similar to how it was done before, now they live in their own class with setter and getter methods for the different slots. Also, unnecessary prefixes and suffixes have been removed, allowing direct connection between results, e.g. tables of marker genes, and the grouping variable they belong to / were derived from. Moreover, additional layers have been added to allow storing results derived from different methods.

Let's look at some details. Overall, the object is organized as such:

```
<Cerebro_object>
├── version (package_version)
├── experiment (named list)
│   ├── experiment_name (string)
│   ├── organism (string)
│   ├── date_of_analysis (string)
│   └── date_of_export (string)
├── technical_info (named list)
├── parameters (named list)
├── groups (named list)
│   └── <grouping_variable> (vector of group levels)
├── cell_cycle (vector)
├── gene_lists (named list)
│   └── <gene_list_name> (vector of genes)
├── expression (matrix-like; attached from the H5 file when an H5-backed .crb is read)
├── expression_backend (list: type "embedded" or "h5", location)
├── crb_schema (list; set for an H5-backed .crb)
├── spatial_molecule_backend (list; set when molecule tables sit in a sibling file)
├── immune_repertoire_backend (list; set when the repertoire sits in a sibling file)
├── cell_fingerprint (identity of the cells, used by saved views)
├── meta_data (data.frame)
├── projections (named list)
│   └── <projection_name> (data.frame)
├── trees (named list)
│   └── <grouping_variable> (phylo)
├── most_expressed_genes (named list)
│   └── <grouping_variable> (data.frame)
├── mean_expression (named list)
│   └── <grouping_variable> (data.frame)
├── marker_genes (named list)
│   └── <method> (named list)
│       └── <table_name> (data.frame)
├── enriched_pathways (named list)
│   └── <method> (named list)
│       └── <table_name> (data.frame)
├── trajectories (named list)
│   └── <method> (named list)
│       └── <trajectory_name> (depends on method, most likely a list or data frame)
├── immune_repertoire (named list)
│   └── <sample> (data.frame, one row per cell with a receptor)
├── hla_typing (data.frame, one row per sample, locus and copy)
├── spatial (named list)
│   └── <section> (list: coordinates, expression, histology_images)
├── trekker (list; Trekker spatial mapping)
└── extra_material (named list)
    ├── tables (named list)
    │   └── <name> (data.frame)    
    └── plots (named list)
        └── <name> (ggplot-object)
```

Interaction with the Cerebro object will be done through internal methods, providing additional control for the correct format of the object.

The expression matrix is either embedded in the `.crb` or kept in an H5 file next to it; `expression_backend` records which (`setExpressionBackend()` accepts only `"embedded"` and `"h5"`), and `saveCerebro()` / `readCerebro()` take care of the rest. T-cell and B-cell receptors live together in `immune_repertoire`; there are no separate `tcr_data` / `bcr_data` fields, and `getTCR()` / `getBCR()` return the TCR or BCR rows of that repertoire. A very large repertoire can sit in a sibling `<stem>.immune.qs2` file that `getImmuneRepertoire()` loads on demand. A `.crb` written by an older release that does not follow this layout is rejected with a pointer to `convertCerebro()`.

As long as you follow the described scheme, you can export and visualize any data frame that is stored in the `marker_genes` or `enriched_pathways` slots. I have prepared a vignette with some more details that you can find [here](https://www.mheming.com/CerebroNexus/articles/tables_and_plots.html).

Please make sure to use names for items in lists, otherwise it will likely result in an error.

The `technical_info` and `parameters` slots hold information about the analysis, such as strings, numbers, and lists that you think are relevant to share; read them with `getTechnicalInfo()` and `getParameters()`. The Viewer uses a few of these entries itself, for example the starting colours of groups (`technical_info$group_colors`) and the grouping variable that projections are coloured by when the data set opens (`parameters$main_group`).

Calling the Cerebro object will give an overview of the information it currently contains, here for the example data set that comes with CerebroNexus:

```{r print-example}
library(CerebroNexus)
crb <- readCerebro(
  system.file("extdata", "examples", "example.crb", package = "CerebroNexus")
)
crb
```

For more details, please check the `Cerebro` reference page.
